To subsidize something means to give it financial support — usually money — so that it can survive, grow, or become cheaper for people to use. The key idea is that without this financial help, the thing being supported would either struggle to exist, fail completely, or become unaffordable.

Think of it like this: imagine a small bakery that makes great bread, but the cost of ingredients is so high that to cover its costs, it would have to charge $20 per loaf — a price almost nobody would pay. Now imagine the government steps in and regularly gives the bakery money to cover part of its costs, so the bakery only needs to charge $5 per loaf. The government has subsidized the bakery.
Who Subsidizes Whom?

There are always two sides:

The subsidizer — the one giving the money. This is most commonly a government, but it can also be a company, an organization, or even a wealthy individual.

The subsidized — the one receiving the support. This could be a business, an industry, a service, a product, or even a person.
Why Does Someone Subsidize?

Subsidizing always happens for a reason or a goal. The subsidizer isn't just giving money away randomly — they want something to happen as a result. Common reasons include:

  • To keep prices affordable for ordinary people (e.g., subsidizing public transport so bus fares stay low)
  • To protect an important industry from collapsing (e.g., subsidizing local farmers so the country doesn't become entirely dependent on imported food)
  • To encourage something that benefits society (e.g., subsidizing solar panels to push people toward clean energy)
  • To help people who can't afford something essential (e.g., subsidizing healthcare or housing for low-income families)

The underlying logic is always: "This thing is valuable or important, but the free market alone won't sustain it properly, so we'll step in financially."
What Does the Financial Support Actually Look Like?

Subsidizing doesn't always mean handing over cash directly, though it can. It can take several forms:

  • Direct cash payments — The government sends money directly to farmers each year.
  • Tax reductions or exemptions — A business pays far less tax than it normally would, which saves it money.
  • Grants — Money given to a university or research lab to fund their work.
  • Reduced-price resources — A government sells land, electricity, or raw materials to a company at below-market prices.
  • Covering part of someone's bill — Health insurance subsidies where the government pays a portion of your monthly premium.

In all these cases, someone is receiving financial benefit they didn't earn through normal commercial activity — and they usually don't have to pay it back. That last point is important.
Subsidizing Is NOT a Loan

This is a critical distinction. When a bank loans you money, you must repay it, usually with interest. A subsidy is different — it is financial support that is not expected to be repaid. The subsidizer gives the money (or the equivalent benefit) because they want the outcome the support produces, not because they expect their money back.
Subsidizing Is Not Pure Charity Either

Charity is driven by goodwill and compassion with no expectation of any return. Subsidizing, while it can be generous in spirit, almost always has a strategic or policy purpose. The subsidizer expects a specific outcome — lower food prices, a stronger local industry, more people using clean energy, etc. It is deliberate and goal-oriented, not just kind-hearted giving.
Real-World Examples to Cement Your Understanding

Example 1 — Agriculture:
Many governments subsidize their farmers. Farming is risky (bad weather, fluctuating prices) and vital to a country's food supply. Without subsidies, many small farms would go bankrupt, and food prices would spike. So the government regularly pays farmers money to keep them in business and food affordable.

Example 2 — Public Transport:
A city's bus or metro system almost never makes enough money from ticket sales alone to cover its full operating costs. The city government subsidizes it — covering the gap — because it wants citizens to have affordable transportation and wants to reduce traffic and pollution.

Example 3 — Education:
When a government subsidizes university education, it pays part of the cost of running universities, allowing students to pay tuition fees that are far lower than the actual cost of their education.

Example 4 — Clean Energy:
A government might subsidize electric cars by giving buyers a discount or rebate, making the cars cheaper to buy. The government absorbs part of the cost because it wants more people to switch away from petrol cars.

Example 5 — Within a Company:
A large company with multiple products can also "cross-subsidize." For example, a tech company might use the enormous profits from its cloud computing division to subsidize its consumer devices — selling phones at near-cost or even at a loss — to gain market share.
The Degree of Subsidizing

You'll often hear phrases like:

  • "heavily subsidized" — the support covers a large portion of the cost (e.g., a country where citizens pay almost nothing for healthcare because the government covers most of it)
  • "partially subsidized" — the support only covers a share of the cost (e.g., a workplace that pays for 50% of your gym membership)
  • "government-subsidized housing" — housing where rent is kept artificially low because the government supports the landlord or the housing program financially
The Controversy Around Subsidizing

Subsidizing is not always universally praised. It has critics and defenders.

Those who support subsidies argue that some industries or services are too important to be left entirely to market forces. A hospital in a rural area may never be "profitable," but people still need healthcare. Subsidizing it makes sense.

Those who criticize subsidies argue that they can distort markets, create unfair competition, make inefficient businesses survive longer than they should, and become a drain on public money. For example, if the government heavily subsidizes a domestic steel industry, foreign steel producers who make steel more efficiently are unfairly disadvantaged.

Understanding this tension will help you read about subsidies in economic and political contexts with far greater clarity.
Related Word Forms

Since you'll encounter this word family regularly:

  • Subsidy (noun) — the actual financial support given. "The farmers received a subsidy from the government."
  • Subsidized (adjective) — describes something that receives or has received this support. "She lives in subsidized housing."
  • Subsidization (noun) — the act or process of subsidizing. "The subsidization of fossil fuels has been controversial."
  • Subsidizer (noun) — the one who gives the subsidy. "The government was the main subsidizer of the arts program."
One-Sentence Summary

To subsidize is to give ongoing financial support to something — a person, business, industry, or service — so that it can exist, survive, or remain affordable, usually because the subsidizer believes it is important or beneficial and wouldn't thrive properly on its own.
